p2c5.essay:
Until now Luzhin has been a voice inside a mother's letter ([[p1c3]]). Here he gets a body, and Dostoevsky dresses it before letting it speak. The long paragraph on his clothes is the cruellest thing in the chapter, because the narrator keeps conceding points: the outfit is 'a perfectly innocent and permissible proceeding', it all 'suited' him, the curled hair does not even look stupid. Each concession sinks him further. A man whose gloves are carried 'for show' and whose hat is held 'too respectfully' has been judged before he opens his mouth, and then he opens it and says 'sojourning'.

The coat speech is the centre. What Luzhin recites is the fashionable doctrine of the 1860s, self-interest promoted to a science, the sort of thing young radicals took from English political economy and from Chernyshevsky. In his mouth it is second-hand and convenient: love yourself first and everyone's coat stays whole. Razumihin is merely bored by it. Raskolnikov is not bored. He lies there 'with a white face and twitching upper lip' and says that the theory, carried out logically, means 'people may be killed'. I read that as more than a debating point. We have heard this arithmetic before, in the tavern of [[p1c6]], where a student proved that one life could be weighed against the general good, and Raskolnikov found the same thought already hatching in his own head. Luzhin is a distorting mirror held up to him: the same premise, smug, bloodless and safe. The fury in the retort is partly recognition.

Meanwhile a second conversation is going on in the same cramped room, and it is the one Raskolnikov is really listening to. Razumihin's sketch of the murderer is exactly right, delivered a yard from the man himself: a beginner who 'lost his head', who took trinkets and missed fifteen hundred roubles in the top drawer. It is the chapter's best joke and its most humiliating moment. Whatever Raskolnikov thought he was doing in [[p1c7]], here it is described as a botch saved by luck.

One fairness to Luzhin. Compare what the letter actually reported with what Raskolnikov throws at him: 'complete control', 'reproach her'. He has sharpened it, and Luzhin's protest about distortion is not wholly dishonest. That does not make him likeable, but it shows how badly Raskolnikov wants a fight. Notice too what Zossimov carries down the stairs with him: the patient wakes up for one subject only.

annotations.quote: Your mamma had commenced a letter to you while I was sojourning in her neighbourhood.
annotations.note: Garnett gives Luzhin 'commenced' and 'sojourning' where anyone else in the room would say 'begun' and 'staying'. He talks like a legal document that has learned to walk, and in this garret, facing Razumihin's 'What do you want?', the register is his first defeat.

annotations.quote: All his clothes were fresh from the tailor’s and were all right, except for being too new and too distinctly appropriate.
annotations.note: A whole character in one qualification. Nothing is wrong with the clothes; what is wrong is that they are a costume for the part of bridegroom, bought for the occasion. Remember that Raskolnikov is lying beside a parcel of second-hand clothes bought for him that same day.

annotations.quote: in a lodging with my friend Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, in the flat of Madame Lippevechsel
annotations.note: Raskolnikov's 'Yes... no' is honest. He knows both names from Marmeladov's tavern monologue in [[p1c2]]: this is the flat where the Marmeladovs live, and Lebeziatnikov is the lodger who beat Katerina Ivanovna. Petersburg is a small place in this novel, and Dostoevsky has just put the fiancé under the drunkard's roof.

annotations.quote: He’s learnt it by heart to show off!
annotations.note: The first thing Raskolnikov says about ideas since his illness, and it is a charge of plagiarism. He is right about Luzhin, who has come to the capital to collect opinions the way he has collected a hat. But the charge that a man is living on borrowed ideas is one this book will not let rest on Luzhin alone.

annotations.quote: It came to my tearing my coat in half to share with my neighbour and we both were left half naked.
annotations.note: The image comes from the legend of St Martin dividing his cloak with a beggar, turned inside out so that charity becomes bad bookkeeping. Luzhin is paraphrasing the 'rational egoism' of the day. Listen to how much he enjoys the word 'science' doing the work conscience used to do.

annotations.quote: He did not know how to rob; he could only murder.
annotations.note: Razumihin, who suspects nothing, produces the most accurate sentence yet spoken about the crime, and says it with the criminal on the sofa. It is also a moral verdict he does not know he is delivering: the practical half of the plan failed and only the killing was carried through.

annotations.quote: carry out logically the theory you were advocating just now, and it follows that people may be killed
annotations.note: The ellipsis that follows in the text matters; he stops himself. This is the closest anyone has come to saying aloud what connects the respectable talk of self-interest to the axe, and the man saying it is not speaking hypothetically. Zossimov's mild 'No, that's not so' is almost comic.

annotations.quote: And even the curve of his spine was expressive of the horrible insult he had received.
annotations.note: Luzhin exits bent double under the low door, protecting his hat. Dostoevsky is often thought of as a novelist of ideas with no eye; sentences like this show the eye was there whenever he wanted comedy.

annotations.quote: he does not respond to anything except one point on which he seems excited--that’s the murder?
annotations.note: The doctor has made the observation a detective would make, and filed it under medicine. For the rest of this Part, watch how the people around Raskolnikov keep noticing exactly the right thing and drawing a kindly conclusion from it.

links.why: The mother's letter, where Luzhin's remark about a poor wife and her benefactor is first reported; compare her wording with what Raskolnikov flings at him here.
The overheard tavern argument about weighing one life against the common good, which is why Luzhin's economics touch a nerve.
Set Razumihin's reconstruction of a first-time criminal who 'lost his head' beside what actually happened in the flat.
Madame Lippevechsel's flat and Lebeziatnikov were both named by Marmeladov in the tavern.

p2c6.essay:
The chapter opens on 'a strange sudden calm', and I distrust it at once, as I think we are meant to. Raskolnikov dresses in the clothes Razumihin bought, pockets his mother's money and walks out with a resolve that has no content: 'all this must be ended to-day', but how, he refuses to think. What follows is a series of auditions for an ending, and the city turns every one of them down.

The first thing I notice is how badly he wants to talk. He asks a stranger whether he likes street music and then describes, with real tenderness, wet snow falling straight down past the lamps. He questions a lad in a red shirt, pushes into a crowd of peasants, lingers among the women outside a dram shop. This is the man who stood on a bridge in [[p2c2]] and felt he had cut himself off from everyone. The cut hurts, it seems, and he keeps pressing on it. Nobody answers him properly. The stranger crosses the street.

Then comes the passage I would mark hardest. Among the prostitutes he remembers reading of a condemned man who would rather stand for eternity on a ledge 'a square yard' wide, in darkness and tempest, than die at once. The source is usually traced to Victor Hugo, but Dostoevsky had no need of a book for it: in 1849 he stood on a parade ground waiting to be shot and was reprieved at the last minute. So the cry 'Only to live, to live and live!' is not decoration. And look at the double turn that follows. 'Man is a vile creature!' is the easy thought. 'And vile is he who calls him vile for that' is the correction, a moment later, and it is the more Dostoevskian half. The square yard of space becomes his private shorthand; it comes back before the chapter is out.

The scene with Zametov is the centre, and it takes place in a restaurant called the Palais de Cristal, the Crystal Palace, which was the emblem of the rational future for the same progressives Luzhin was quoting an hour ago. I cannot believe the name is innocent. Raskolnikov has come to read about himself in the newspapers and ends by performing himself for a police clerk. He tries out verbs for it, 'I declare', 'I confess', 'I make a deposition', like a man choosing a hat. Why does he do it? I see three impulses that he cannot separate: the urge to jeer from behind the door, which the narrator ties explicitly to the latch in [[p1c7]]; a plain craving to be rid of the secret; and a gambler's instinct that the boldest move is the safest. The dreadful comedy is that the third one works. He describes hiding the loot under a stone, which is the literal truth, and asks 'what if it was I', and Zametov walks away convinced that the lieutenant who suspected him is 'a blockhead'. The truth, said outright, serves as an alibi. The narrator insists he did this 'unwittingly', and I believe it. Notice also that he waves his banknotes at Zametov seconds after sneering that the police only catch men who suddenly have money.

Razumihin on the steps is the relief and the rebuke. His 'go to hell then' is said 'gently', and his tirade against people who are 'plagiarists' even in their suffering, each one 'a translation' and not 'an original', hits a man whose great idea we first heard from a stranger in a tavern. Razumihin does not know that. He just wants him to come to the party.

After that the endings are tried in earnest. A woman climbs the railing beside him and drops into the canal, and what he sees is not tragedy but a skirt 'inflated like a balloon', a rescue with a pole, sneezing. 'It's not good enough.' So, the police. But his feet take him to 'the' house instead, and the flat is being repapered with lilac flowers, which annoys him 'horribly', as if the place had no right to recover. He rings the cracked bell three times to get the terror back and finds that it gives him 'satisfaction'. He asks about the blood. He all but orders the porters to march him to the station, and they throw him into the street as a nuisance. That is the pattern of the whole evening: he offers himself, and no one will take him. He stands at the crossroads waiting for 'a decisive word', and the stones say nothing.

annotations.quote: when wet snow is falling straight down, when there’s no wind--you know what I mean?--and the street lamps shine through it
annotations.note: A murderer, a few hours out of a three-day delirium, confiding his taste in weather to a stranger. The detail is lovely and exact, which is what frightens the man. That 'you know what I mean?' is a plea; he wants one person in Petersburg to share a sensation with him.

annotations.quote: Only to live, to live and live! Life, whatever it may be!
annotations.note: He has come out to 'make an end', and standing among the bruised women of the dram shops he finds himself arguing the opposite case. Dostoevsky knew the condemned man's arithmetic at first hand from his own mock execution in 1849. Keep the ledge in mind; Raskolnikov will refer to it again as if it were a known address.

annotations.quote: to put out his tongue at them, to mock them, to laugh, and laugh, and laugh!
annotations.note: The narrator reaches back to the worst minute of [[p1c7]], the men rattling the door, and reveals something that scene only hinted at: part of him wanted to give himself away for the fun of it. The laughter in the restaurant is the same impulse, and it is not under his control.

annotations.quote: I would lift that stone--there would sure to be a hollow under it, and I would put the jewels and money in that hole.
annotations.note: Every word is a report of what he did in [[p2c2]], shifted into the conditional. Garnett's 'there would sure to be' is a slip of grammar she let stand. The one invented detail is the patience: 'a year or two, three maybe'. He has not looked at what he took.

annotations.quote: The terrible word trembled on his lips, like the latch on that door
annotations.note: The sentence goes on into the present tense, 'it will break out', as though the narrator had lost his own distance for a second. And the simile makes the confession and the crime one event: the word inside his mouth is himself behind the door, with someone shaking the handle.

annotations.quote: “Ilya Petrovitch is a blockhead,” he decided.
annotations.note: The practical result of the scene. Zametov reasons that no guilty man would behave like that, so the suspicion bred by the fainting fit in [[p2c1]] must be nonsense. It is a sound inference about ordinary criminals and wrong about this one.

annotations.quote: if you were an original instead of a translation
annotations.note: Razumihin earns part of his living translating, so the insult comes from his own trade. He means a generation that takes even its despair second-hand. It makes a pair with Raskolnikov's sneer at Luzhin in [[p2c5]] for having 'learnt it by heart'.

annotations.quote: No, that’s loathsome... water... it’s not good enough
annotations.note: He had been leaning on that rail and the water had 'seemed to catch his attention'. Then a stranger does it in front of him and is fished out sneezing. Suicide is rejected on what sounds like aesthetic grounds, which tells you how much vanity survives in him even now.

annotations.quote: He shuddered at every ring and it gave him more and more satisfaction.
annotations.note: That tinny bell has been in his ears since [[p1c1]]; the 'cracked note' is the same one. Here he rings it to summon the terror back, and enjoys it. I find this the most disturbing sentence in the chapter: he would rather feel that evening again than feel nothing.

annotations.quote: all was dead and silent like the stones on which he walked, dead to him, to him alone
annotations.note: He is standing at a cross-roads, and the narrator makes him wait there for 'a decisive word' from outside. None comes. The phrase 'to him alone' is the important part: the city is noisy enough for everyone else.

links.why: The trembling latch and the cracked bell that this chapter deliberately replays.
The stone in the yard and the bridge where he felt severed from everyone; his 'hypothetical' to Zametov is this chapter retold.
The fainting fit in the police office that he now taunts Zametov with.
He stops at the Hay Market corner where the huckster and his wife talked with Lizaveta, the chance overhearing that fixed the hour.

p2c7.essay:
It matters that this chapter begins as an interruption. Raskolnikov had 'fully made up his mind' to go to the police, and he walks toward the carriage almost idly, clutching at one more distraction. Then the lantern shows him Marmeladov's face and he becomes a different person: quick, practical, shouting 'I'll pay' half a dozen times. The money is what remains of his mother's remittance from [[p2c3]]. He pleads 'as earnestly as if it had been his father', and for the first time since the murder he is doing something whose meaning he does not have to work out.

Katerina Ivanovna is the best thing here, and she is harder than her husband's tavern portrait in [[p1c2]] prepared me for. Dostoevsky will not make the deathbed edifying. Her memories of the marshal's ball are interrupted by instructions about darning; she fights the landlady over a patronymic while her husband bleeds on the sofa; and when the priest offers the usual words she answers him with laundry. 'I have forgiven as it is!' is not a refusal. She means that forgiveness, in this room, is something done nightly at a basin of water and has nothing to do with saying so. Twice she silences Marmeladov when he tries to ask for it. Then she shows the priest the blood on her handkerchief and he has nothing to say.

Sonia has been talked about since the second chapter of the book and arrives without a line. She stands in the doorway in her working clothes, the crinoline filling the frame, and her father has 'never seen her before in such attire'. That is the sentence that undoes me. His last word is 'Forgive!' and it is addressed to her.

What I would hold on to is the aftermath. Raskolnikov leaves 'covered with blood', says so to the police superintendent with a smile, and feels like 'a man condemned to death who has suddenly been pardoned'. A child hugs him and he asks to be prayed for. Back on the bridge he announces 'the reign of reason and light', of 'will' and 'strength'. Look at what revived him: giving away twenty roubles and being kissed by a ten-year-old. Look at what he credits: strength. The narrator notices the gap ('perhaps he was in too great a hurry with his conclusions') and so, half-laughing, does he. And then the light under his own door. He could stare down Zametov an hour ago. Faced with his mother's arms, 'he could not'.

annotations.quote: with his legs stretched out straight before him--heels together and toes turned out
annotations.note: The little boy waiting to have his only shirt taken off for the wash. Dostoevsky comes back to this pose after the men carry the body in, the child still sitting to attention in the middle of the catastrophe. Small, exact observations of children are where this novelist is gentlest.

annotations.quote: You must mend that tear, you must take your needle and darn it as I showed you
annotations.note: A parenthesis dropped into the middle of the shawl dance and the princess. Her two lives run in the same sentence, the remembered ballroom and the darning, and the cough cuts across both. The grand past may be embroidered; the tear in the shirt certainly is not.

annotations.quote: that strange inner feeling of satisfaction which may be observed in the presence of a sudden accident
annotations.note: The narrator steps out of the scene to state a general law, and extends it to 'those nearest and dearest'. It is unflattering and I think true. It also bears on the excited young man who has just carried the victim upstairs.

annotations.quote: I have you once before told that you to call me Amalia Ludwigovna may not dare; I am Amalia Ivanovna.
annotations.note: Garnett renders the landlady's broken Russian by keeping German word order in English. The quarrel is about a patronymic: 'Ivanovna' sounds Russian and respectable, 'Ludwigovna' advertises the foreigner. Katerina Ivanovna knows precisely which one stings, and uses it over a dying man.

annotations.quote: the absurd round straw hat with its flaring flame-coloured feather
annotations.note: We have seen this feather before, earlier the same evening, on the fifteen-year-old street singer in [[p2c6]]. The repetition is deliberate: it is the uniform of girls sent out to earn. Sonia 'forgot' she was wearing any of it, which tells you what she ran here as.

annotations.quote: What’s the use of talking of forgiveness! I have forgiven as it is!
annotations.note: Her answer to the priest, and the theological centre of the chapter as far as I am concerned. Forgiveness for her is what she was going to do tonight anyway: wash his shirt. Against that, the priest's 'words and only words' have nothing to stand on.

annotations.quote: Raskolnikov said with a peculiar air; then he smiled, nodded and went downstairs.
annotations.note: He has just agreed that he is 'covered with blood', to the head of the district police, and he enjoys the double meaning. This blood was got by helping. I think he half believes for a moment that the one can be set against the other.

annotations.quote: that of a man condemned to death who has suddenly been pardoned
annotations.note: The condemned man again, an hour or two after the ledge in [[p2c6]], and this time the image is the author's own biography: Dostoevsky was reprieved in front of a firing squad in 1849. Note that nothing in Raskolnikov's legal position has changed at all.

annotations.quote: Perhaps he was in too great a hurry with his conclusions, but he did not think of that.
annotations.note: A rare dry aside from a narrator who usually stays inside Raskolnikov's fever. He has just compared him to 'a man catching at a straw'. We are being told, quietly, not to trust the triumph on the bridge.

annotations.quote: He did not lift his arms to embrace them, he could not.
annotations.note: All the 'strength' of the bridge speech lasts until the two people he loves touch him. The narrator's own question in the paragraph before is the right one: why had he 'never expected, never thought of them'? He had been told that very day they were coming.

links.why: Marmeladov's tavern confession, where this room, this wife, these children and this daughter were all described in advance.
The same bridge, the square yard of space and the first flame-coloured feather, from earlier this same evening.
The mother's letter announcing the journey that ends at his door tonight.
The scene in the garret runs straight on; read the next chapter without a break.
